title: Thread pool and Thread lifecycle
summary: Thread states are the JVM's scheduling contract; a thread pool is admission control on top of it. Master the transitions, the core-queue-max rule, and the failure modes.

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: A thread pool does not make your task faster. It makes overload survivable. The lifecycle — `NEW`, `RUNNABLE`, `BLOCKED`, `WAITING`, `TIMED_WAITING`, `TERMINATED` — tells you *where* a task is stuck. The pool — workers plus bounded queue plus rejection policy — decides *what happens when there is more work than threads*. If you cannot read the first, you cannot tune the second. Every pool bug is a lifecycle bug with a queue in front of it.
What thread lifecycle and thread pool actually are

A Java thread has exactly six observable states exposed by `Thread.State`. That enum is not documentation, it is a contract between the JVM scheduler and the operating system scheduler about why a thread is not making progress right now. `NEW` means the `Thread` object exists but no OS thread has been allocated. `RUNNABLE` means the thread is eligible to run — it may be running on a core or waiting in the OS run queue, Java cannot distinguish the two. `BLOCKED` means it wants a monitor lock held by someone else. `WAITING` means it voluntarily parked itself until another thread signals it. `TIMED_WAITING` means the same but with a deadline. `TERMINATED` means the stack has unwound and the native thread is gone; the transition is one-way and `start()` can never be called again on that object. That is the whole lifecycle. Everything else is a method that moves you between those boxes.

items: `NEW` — object allocated, `start()` not yet called. Holds no OS resources. Calling `run()` here does nothing concurrent; it just executes in the caller thread.
`RUNNABLE` — after `start()`, before death. Includes actually-running plus ready-to-run. A thread spinning in a tight loop and a thread preempted by the OS both report `RUNNABLE`.
`BLOCKED` — stuck at a `synchronized` entry or `Object.wait` re-entry because another thread owns the monitor. Holds no monitor while blocked; it is purely contended.

`WAITING` — parked indefinitely via `Object.wait()` with no timeout, `Thread.join()` with no timeout, or `LockSupport.park()`. Releases the monitor if entered via `wait()`, keeps it if parked via other primitives. Needs an explicit signal.

`TIMED_WAITING` — parked with a deadline via `Thread.sleep()`, `wait(timeout)`, `join(timeout)`, `parkNanos()`, or blocking-queue poll with timeout. Wakes on signal *or* expiry. `sleep()` never releases any lock, which is why sleeping while holding a lock is a design smell.
`TERMINATED` — `run()` returned normally or threw. Native resources released. `isAlive()` is false. The object remains as a tombstone for `join()` callers and retained state.

blocks.text: A thread pool is a deliberate refusal to map one task to one thread. Creating a thread costs a native thread plus a commit of stack memory — typically hundreds of kilobytes to a megabyte — plus scheduler registration and GC-root scanning. Destroying it costs syscalls and churn. Under burst load that cost dominates. So a pool keeps `N` long-lived workers alive in a loop of take-task, run-task, repeat, and feeds them from a queue. The queue absorbs burst. The bound on workers caps context switching and memory. The rejection policy defines overload behavior explicitly instead of collapsing the host. Why this shape wins: reuse amortizes creation cost and bounds concurrency to what the CPU, memory, and downstream dependencies can actually sustain. Trade-off: you add queueing delay and the risk of deadlock-by-pool, where tasks waiting in the queue depend on tasks already occupying every worker.

Only a few methods move a thread, and each has precise lock semantics you must memorize. `start()` moves `NEW` to `RUNNABLE` once; a second call throws. Entering a contended `synchronized` block moves `RUNNABLE` to `BLOCKED`; acquiring the monitor moves it back. That is the only path into `BLOCKED`, which is why `BLOCKED` always means lock contention and never means I/O or sleep. `Object.wait()` atomically releases the monitor and moves to `WAITING` or `TIMED_WAITING`; `notify()` or `notifyAll()` plus re-acquiring the lock moves it back to `RUNNABLE`. `Thread.sleep()` and `LockSupport.park()` do not release anything — the thread keeps every lock it holds while parked, which is why holding a lock across `sleep()` serializes the whole pool. `Thread.join()` parks the *caller*, not the target. `interrupt()` does not kill anything; it only sets a flag and wakes sleepers and waiters with an exception. The thread must cooperate by checking the flag or propagating the exception. Misunderstanding this is the source of most hung-shutdown bugs.

blocks.title: Thread lifecycle transitions
blocks.caption: The six Thread.State values and the calls that move between them.
blocks.code:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> NEW
  NEW --> RUNNABLE : start
  RUNNABLE --> BLOCKED : contended sync entry
  BLOCKED --> RUNNABLE : monitor acquired
  RUNNABLE --> WAITING : wait join park
  WAITING --> RUNNABLE : notify unpark join done
  RUNNABLE --> TIMED_WAITING : sleep wait timeout
  TIMED_WAITING --> RUNNABLE : timeout interrupt signal
  RUNNABLE --> TERMINATED : run returns
  BLOCKED --> RUNNABLE : interrupt still waits for lock
  WAITING --> RUNNABLE : interrupt with exception

blocks.text: `ThreadPoolExecutor` is not magic; it is a counter, a queue, and a worker loop with a strict offer order. On `execute()`, if fewer than `corePoolSize` workers exist, it spawns a new worker immediately even if the queue is empty. Otherwise it tries `queue.offer()`. Only if the queue is full *and* fewer than `maximumPoolSize` workers exist does it spawn an extra worker. Only if the queue is full *and* max workers exist does it invoke the rejection handler. Read that twice: by default the pool prefers queueing over growing. That is why a pool constructed with an unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue` never grows past core size — the queue never reports full, so max is dead config. The worker loop itself is `while (running) { task = getTask(); task.run(); }` where `getTask()` is a blocking poll with `keepAliveTime` timeout for non-core threads. Shutdown is cooperative: `shutdown()` stops accepting and drains, `shutdownNow()` interrupts workers and returns the drained list, but neither forcibly kills a thread ignoring interrupts. Why this design: it optimizes for stable throughput under sustained load at the cost of added latency under burst. Trade-off: you must size all four knobs together — core, max, queue capacity, and rejection — or one of them silently disables the others.

blocks.title: Thread pool admission path
blocks.caption: Every submit follows core, then queue, then max, then reject. No exceptions.
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
    S[submit execute] --> D{workers LT core}
    D -->|yes| C[create core worker]
    D -->|no| Q{queue offer ok}
    Q -->|yes| B[enqueue wait]
    Q -->|no| M{workers LT max}
    M -->|yes| E[create extra worker]
    M -->|no| R[RejectedExecutionHandler]
    C --> W[worker run loop]
    E --> W
    B --> W

blocks.text: Sizing is admission control, not performance tuning. `corePoolSize` is the steady-state concurrency you will pay for even when idle. `maximumPoolSize` is the burst concurrency you are willing to pay for under pressure. Queue capacity is how much latency you will accept before you start paying for burst or shedding load. `keepAliveTime` is how fast you release burst capacity afterward. A small core with a large queue minimizes thread churn and protects downstream systems but lets tail latency grow linearly with queue depth. A large max with a `SynchronousQueue` — effectively zero capacity — minimizes queueing delay but spawns threads aggressively and thrashes on bursty I/O. Direct handoff only makes sense when tasks are short and independent. There is no universal size. The correct bound comes from the bottleneck: CPU, lock, or downstream socket. Trade-off stated plainly: every slot you add for throughput is a slot that can pile onto a saturated dependency and make the outage worse.

blocks.caption: Pool shapes and what each one costs you.
rows: Fixed pool + bounded queue + CallerRuns or Abort
Predictable memory, backpressure, no silent growth
Caller blocks or fails fast; must handle rejection at call site
Cached pool / unbounded max
Low latency for short bursty tasks
Unbounded thread creation under load; OOM and context-switch collapse
Unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue with large max
Never rejects; simple mental model
Max is dead code; queue grows until heap dies; latency hides overload
SynchronousQueue + large max
No queue delay; true elasticity for fast tasks
Thread explosion if tasks block on I/O or locks
Single-thread executor
Total ordering, no races, trivial reasoning
Zero parallelism; one stuck task halts the pipeline
ForkJoinPool / work-stealing
Good for divisible recursive CPU work
Terrible for blocking I/O; steals hide starvation and complicate dumps

blocks.text: How it fails in production, and the symptom you would see

Pool failures never announce themselves as pool failures. They show up as rising p99, stuck shutdowns, or a host that stops responding while CPU sits idle. The pattern to internalize: threads are not work, they are slots. When every slot is parked waiting for something that itself needs a slot, the system is deadlocked regardless of CPU headroom. When the queue is unbounded, the symptom is not rejection but a slow memory leak that looks like a GC problem until you dump the queue depth. When tasks swallow interrupts, `shutdownNow()` returns but workers never die and deploys hang. Learn to distinguish `BLOCKED` — many threads blocked on the same monitor address means a hot lock — from `WAITING` on a pool queue — idle workers are healthy — from `WAITING` on a future inside a pool task — that is pool-induced deadlock in progress. The thread dump is the only ground truth; metrics only tell you where to look.

blocks.caption: Failure to symptom to fix. Memorize the middle column.
rows: Pool deadlock: task submits and joins on same pool
All workers `WAITING` on `Future.get`, queue full, CPU idle, p99 infinite
Never block on a child from same pool; use separate pool or CompletableFuture chain
Unbounded queue overload
Heap grows, GC pauses climb, latency climbs for hours then OOM
Bound the queue; add Abort or CallerRuns; alert on queue depth, not just threads
Hot monitor / synchronized bottleneck
Many threads `BLOCKED` on identical lock address in dump
Shrink critical section, split lock, or switch contended path to ReentrantLock or concurrent structure
Interrupt-swallowing tasks
`shutdownNow` returns but JVM never exits; threads stuck `TIMED_WAITING` in sleep
Propagate InterruptedException, restore flag with `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`, check flag in loops
Thread leak: new pool per request
Thread count climbs monotonically; native OOM despite free heap
Share one injected executor; name threads; meter created vs destroyed workers
CallerRuns under sustained overload
Latency propagates to front-end threads; entire server slows coherently
That is backpressure working; add timeout + bulkhead, do not just raise max

blocks.text: Diagnosis in practice is thirty seconds with a dump. Capture two `jstack` outputs five seconds apart. Ignore threads in `RUNNABLE` inside socket read — those are I/O bound, not CPU bound. Focus on identical stacks: twenty workers `BLOCKED` on the same `locked <0xabc>` line is a contended lock, fix the lock holder first. Twenty workers `WAITING` at `LinkedBlockingQueue.take` is a healthy idle pool, not a leak. Twenty workers `TIMED_WAITING` at `Future.get` with tasks queued behind them is the pool waiting on itself — the classic self-deadlock. Why dumps beat logging here: state plus stack shows *why* progress stopped, while throughput metrics only show that it did. Trade-off: dumps are a point sample; always take two to separate transient parking from a stuck set.
Sizing: the only formula that survives contact

Start from the bottleneck, not from core count. If tasks are CPU-bound with no blocking, `cores + 1` is the ceiling — more threads only add context switches and cache misses. If tasks block on I/O, apply Little's law: threads needed roughly equals throughput times average blocking time plus cores. A service doing 200 requests per second each blocking 100ms on a downstream socket needs about 20 slots just to stay even, before headroom. That formula assumes tasks are independent. The moment tasks share a lock, contend on a connection pool, or submit to each other, the math collapses and the real limit is the scarcest shared resource. So size the pool to protect that resource: connection pool of 20 means worker max near 20, not 200. Always bound the queue to a multiple of throughput times your latency budget — if you cannot drain within your p99 SLO, you should reject, not enqueue. Trade-off: precise sizing buys efficiency but couples you to one workload; slightly over-provisioned core with aggressive timeouts buys robustness across workloads at the cost of idle memory.
How it shows up in an interview

items.title: Draw the six states without notes
items.text: Expected in under two minutes. Say what holds a lock in each state. Interviewers fail candidates who conflate BLOCKED with WAITING. State the rule: BLOCKED is only monitor entry, WAITING is explicit parking, TIMED_WAITING adds a deadline.

items.title: Explain wait vs sleep vs park vs join
items.text: They want lock semantics, not definitions. Answer: wait releases, sleep never releases, park is permit-based and needs no monitor, join parks the caller. Mention spurious wakeups and the while-loop guard.

items.title: Design a fixed pool from scratch
items.text: Sketch BlockingQueue plus N workers looping on take and running tasks. Handle poison pill or interrupt for shutdown, rejection when bounded and full, and exception containment so one bad task does not kill a worker. Do not reach for raw Thread per request.

items.title: Defend core, max, queue, and rejection
items.text: Walk the execute path in order: core first, then queue, then max, then reject. Explain why unbounded queue disables max and why CallerRuns is backpressure while Abort forces the caller to handle overload. Pick values for a CPU-bound vs IO-bound example.

items.title: Debug a stuck pool live
items.text: Given a dump with all workers WAITING on Future.get, diagnose self-deadlock. Propose the fix: separate pools for parent and child, timeout on get, or async chaining. Mention interrupt cooperation for clean shutdown.

items: `RUNNABLE` means running on a CPU. It does not. It means eligible. A thread descheduled by the OS still reports `RUNNABLE`. Only profiling plus dumps separate spinning from starved.
`Calling run() starts a thread.` It does not. It executes synchronously in the caller. Only `start()` allocates a new call stack and moves `NEW` to `RUNNABLE`.
`BLOCKED` and `WAITING` are interchangeable words for stuck. They are not. `BLOCKED` always implicates a `synchronized` monitor; `WAITING` implicates coordination. Different cause, different fix.
`interrupt()` stops a thread. It only requests. If code catches `InterruptedException` and continues, or never checks the flag, the thread ignores you and shutdown hangs.
`sleep()` releases locks like `wait()` does. Opposite. `sleep()` keeps every monitor. Sleeping while holding a lock serializes all contenders for the duration.
`More threads means more throughput.` Past the bottleneck it means more contention, more memory, and worse tail latency. Throughput is capped by the scarcest shared resource, not by worker count.

`An unbounded queue is safer because it never rejects.` It is the least safe choice. It converts overload into unbounded heap growth and hides the signal until GC collapse. Bounded plus explicit rejection fails fast and visibly.

blocks.caption: When a pool helps and when it hurts.
headers: Avoid a pool, do this instead
rows: Many short independent tasks share a host: request handling, background jobs
One long-lived ordered stream: use a single thread to guarantee ordering
You need to bound concurrency to protect CPU or downstream sockets
Tasks are strictly sequential and dependent: use async chaining, not blocking get on same pool
Tasks are homogeneous enough to share sizing and timeout policy
Tasks have wildly different SLAs: split into separate pools so slow tasks cannot starve fast ones
Overload must shed or slow callers explicitly via rejection
Burst is rare and tiny: direct handoff or virtual threads may be simpler than tuning core-max-queue
Lifecycle must be managed: graceful drain, naming, metrics, saturation alerts
Lifetime is the whole process: a dedicated long-lived thread with a clear ownership model beats a pool

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: **Thread lifecycle is six states describing why a thread is not progressing; a pool reuses a bounded set of workers over a bounded queue so overload becomes explicit rejection instead of collapse — size core for steady load, max for burst, queue for latency budget, and never block a pool task on the same pool.**

blocks.title: Shutdown is part of the design
blocks.text: A pool you cannot stop is a leak. Always expose `shutdown()` plus `awaitTermination()` with a timeout, propagate interrupts, name threads so dumps are readable, and meter queue depth and active count. If the interviewer does not ask about shutdown, bring it up yourself — it signals production experience.
